stories.title: El mercado
stories.text:
María va al mercado con su hija Ana. El mercado está en la plaza, al lado de la escuela. Hay muchas frutas: manzanas, naranjas y plátanos.

— Ana, ¿qué quieres comprar?
— Quiero tres naranjas, mamá.
— Muy bien. También necesito pan para la familia. ¿Cómo está el tiempo?
— Está muy bonito hoy.

María compra las naranjas, un kilo de manzanas y agua. Paga ocho euros. Ana ayuda a su madre y después van a casa. En casa, el perro está esperando. Ana le da una naranja. El perro está muy feliz.

María está cansada pero feliz. Mañana vuelve al mercado con su amiga Elena.

explanation.en: 'María está cansada pero feliz' — tired but happy. Note estar for feelings here.

stories.title: La casa de Carlos
stories.text:
Carlos vive en una casa azul. La casa es pequeña pero muy bonita. Carlos es alto y pelo negro. Tiene una hermana que se llama Lucía.

Los sábados Carlos no trabaja. Sus amigos están en la casa. Están en el jardín con el perro. El perro es blanco y muy pequeño.

Lucía cocina. Carlos pone la mesa y habla con su amigo Pablo. Hoy están felices porque mañana van a la playa.

— Carlos, ¿está tu hermana?
— Sí, Lucía está en la cocina.

Por la noche la familia está junta. La casa está limpia y el tiempo es bueno.

stories.title: El primer encuentro
stories.text:
— Buenos días. Me llamo Nora. ¿Cómo estás?
— Muy bien, gracias. Me llamo Luis.
— Encantado, Luis. ¿De dónde eres?
— Soy de Sevilla, pero ahora vivo en Madrid. ¿Y tú?
— Soy de Lima. Vivo aquí desde hace dos años.
— Qué bien. ¿Hablas español con tus amigos?
— Sí, hablo español todos los días. A veces hablo inglés también.
— Muy bien. Adiós, Luis.
— Adiós, Nora. Hasta luego.

stories.title: En la tienda
stories.text:
— Buenos días. ¿Cuántas botas quiere?
— Dos, por favor. ¿Cuánto cuestan?
— Cuestan ochenta euros.
— Bien. Y quiero una mochila azul también.
— La mochila cuesta cincuenta euros. Todo son ciento treinta euros.
— Perfecto. Y una bolsa, por favor.
— Aquí tiene. ¡Que tenga un buen día!

stories.title: La bicicleta nueva
stories.text:
Ana tiene una bicicleta nueva. La bicicleta es azul y el asiento es negro.
— ¿De qué color es tu bicicleta? —pregunta su amigo.
— Azul —responde Ana—. Antes era roja, pero ahora es azul.— ¿Y el casco?
— El casco es amarillo. Y las luces son blancas.
Ana está muy feliz. Su bicicleta es bonita y las ruedas son negras.

stories.title: En la clase
stories.text:
En la clase de español hay doce estudiantes. Todos hablan un poco.
La profesora se llama Elena y habla muy rápido.
— Buenos días —dice ella—. Hoy estudiamos los verbos.
— Yo estudio español todos los días —dice Marta—. Estudio dos horas.
— Nosotros estudiamos juntos —dicen Pedro y Ana—. Ellos estudian en la biblioteca.
— ¿Dónde estudias tú, Pablo?
— Estudio en casa. Y a veces estudio en la biblioteca.
— Muy bien. Hablad español en la clase, por favor.

stories.title: La comida
stories.text:
Carlos vive en una casa pequeña pero bonita. Todos los días come bien.
— ¿Qué comes, Carlos?
— Como verduras y fruta. Y como pan con queso.
— ¿Dónde vives?
— Vivo cerca del parque. Mi hermana vive en el centro y ella come en restaurantes.
— ¿Qué come tu hermana?
— Ella come pescado y bebe café. Nosotros comemos en casa.
— ¿Y tus amigos?
— Mis amigos comen en la cafetería. Todos comemos bien.

stories.title: La familia
stories.text:
Mi familia es grande. Somos cinco: mi madre, mi padre, mi hermana, mi hermano y yo.
Mi padre es profesor y mi madre es médica. Mi hermana está en la escuela y mi hermano está en casa.
Nosotros tenemos un perro. El perro es pequeño y blanco.
— ¿Dónde está tu padre? —pregunta mi madre.
— Está en el trabajo. Siempre está allí.
— ¿Y tus amigos?
— Mis amigos están en el parque. Van allí todos los días.
Mi familia es feliz.

stories.title: La cita
stories.text:
— ¿Cuándo es tu cumpleaños, Elena?
— Es el quince de marzo. Este año es el tres de marzo.
— ¿A qué hora es la fiesta?
— Empieza a las ocho y media de la noche.
— Perfecto. Yo llego a las ocho menos cuarto.
— ¿Y tu hermano?
— Mi hermano llega a las nueve en punto. Siempre llega tarde.
— Bueno. Nos vemos el quince de marzo.

stories.title: En el café
stories.text:
— Buenos días. ¿Qué quiere tomar?
— Un café, por favor. Y una tostada.
— Muy bien. ¿Algo más?
— No, gracias. Eso es todo. ¿Sabe usted dónde está la estación?
— Sí, está cerca. Pero no puede ir ahora: la calle está cerrada.
— Vale. Entonces vengo mañana.
— Perfecto. Hasta mañana.
— Gracias. Adiós.

stories.title: La rutina
stories.text:
Me levanto a las siete todos los días. Me ducho y bebo un café.
Mi hermana se levanta más tarde. Ella no se ducha por la mañana: se ducha por la noche.
Nosotros nos acostamos tarde. Ellos se acuestan a las once.
— ¿A qué hora te quedas tú en casa?
— Yo me quedo en casa los domingos. Después me acuesto muy pronto.
— Nosotros no nos quedamos en casa. Salimos.

stories.title: El verano pasado
stories.text:
El verano pasado fui a la playa con mi familia. Salimos de Madrid muy temprano, porque el coche estaba en el taller.
La casa estaba en un pueblo pequeño. Todos los días nadábamos en la piscina por la mañana y por la tarde caminábamos por la playa.
Un día llovió. No pudimos ir a la playa, pero estuvimos en la casa todo el día. Mi madre cocinó paella y mi padre bebió vino.
La última noche del viaje no dormimos: hablamos hasta las tres.
Al año siguiente repetimos el viaje. Volvimos en agosto y lo pasamos igual de bien.

stories.title: El informe
stories.text:
Ayer terminé un proyecto muy importante. Duró seis meses.
La reunión con mi jefa fue el lunes. Ella me preguntó por el informe y yo le respondí con los números.
No sabía si los resultados eran buenos, pero parecían buenos.
Ella no dijo nada durante un minuto. Luego dijo: «Hiciste un buen trabajo».
Ese día salí de la oficina a las ocho. Normalmente salía a las seis, así que fue un regalo.
Al mes siguiente empecé otro proyecto. Esta vez era más difícil.

stories.title: Los planes
stories.text:
Marta tiene planes para el verano. Dentro de un mes empiezan las vacaciones.
— ¿Qué harás este verano? —le pregunta su hermana.
— No lo sé todavía. Quizá trabaje, o quizá descanse.
— ¿Vas a viajar?
— Sí, ya reservé el billete. Iremos a Lisboa en agosto.
— Perfecto. ¿Reservaste el hotel?
— Todavía no. Y seguro que lo haré mañana, porque los hoteles en agosto se llenan rápido.
Marta espera que todo salga bien. Si el trabajo se acaba pronto, tendrá más días libres. Si no, irá sola y no pasa nada.

stories.title: ¿Podrías abrirme?

titleTranslations.en: Could you open it for me?

stories.text:
— Perdone, ¿podría abrirme la puerta? El ascensor no funciona.
— Claro, espere un momento.
El hombre le abrió la puerta y después subió con ella al quinto piso.
— Gracias. ¿Sabe usted cuándo lo arreglarán?
— Creo que mañana por la mañana. Siempre se rompe entre semana.
— ¿Y si no lo arreglan? Tendré que subir andando todos los días.
— No se preocupe. Seguramente estará funcionando antes del lunes.
Ella le dio las gracias otra vez y entró en su piso.

stories.title: La fábrica
stories.text:
La fábrica está en el barrio nuevo. Es una fábrica grande y es muy antigua.
El jefe se llama Herrán y es de Madrid. Su mujer, Klara, es polaca y trabaja en una escuela.
Hoy es lunes y la fábrica está cerrada. No hay nadie dentro.
— ¿Por qué está cerrada la fábrica?
— Porque el jefe está de vacaciones. Toda la semana.
— ¿Y los trabajadores?
— Están en casa. Todos están enfadados, porque la fábrica lleva dos semanas rota.
La semana pasada la máquina no funcionaba. Nadie sabía qué pasaba. Y no tenían miedo: tenían prisa.
A ver qué pasa cuando vuelva el jefe.

stories.title: Un mal día
stories.text:
Me desperté tarde y tenía mucha hambre. No había leche, así que no había desayuno.
Salí a la calle y hacía frío. El cielo estaba lleno de nubes y llovía.
Volví a casa mojado. Empecé a trabajar, y a las once me sentí fatal.
Me dolía la cabeza y tenía fiebre. No tenía ganas de nada.
A las dos me acosté un rato. A las cuatro me desperté con más hambre todavía.
Por la noche comí paella y me sentí mucho mejor.
Al día siguiente seguía cansado, pero ya no tenía fiebre.

stories.title: El mercado del sábado
stories.text:
Los sábados por la mañana voy al mercado con mi hermana. Está cerca de nuestra casa y abre a las ocho.
Primero vamos a la frutería. Compramos fruta: dos kilos de naranjas, un kilo de plátanos y cuatro manzanas. La fruta de aquí es barata y buena.
Después vamos a la carnicería. Mi hermana compra pollo y yo compro queso. El queso es caro, pero está bueno.
— ¿Quieres carne? —pregunta ella.
— No, hoy no. Tenemos pollo de ayer.
— Bueno. Pagamos y nos vamos. No quiero estar aquí mucho tiempo.
De vuelta compramos pan. El pan es lo único que nunca tenemos suficiente en casa.
A la una ya estamos en casa.

stories.title: En el restaurante
stories.text:
El sábado por la noche vamos mi hermana y yo a un restaurante italiano cerca de casa. La camarera nos trae el menú.
— Buenas noches. ¿Qué va a tomar?
— Para mí, una sopa y el pescado. ¿Y tú?
— El pollo con arroz, por favor. Y un agua.
— Muy bien. Un momento.
La comida estuvo buena. El pescado era pequeño, pero estaba muy rico.
— ¿Tomamos postre?
— Sí. Yo quiero helado. Ella prefiere café.
— Perfecto. La cuenta, por favor.
La camarera trae la cuenta. Mi hermana paga y deja una propina del diez por ciento.
— Buen provecho —dice ella.

stories.title: El primer día
stories.text:
El lunes pasado empecé en un trabajo nuevo. La empresa está en un edificio
pequeño, cerca de la estación. Mi jefe se llama Ricardo y lleva diez años
en la empresa.

Llegué a las ocho y media. Una chica me trajo un café y me explicó dónde
estaba la sala. Al principio no conocía a nadie, pero al mediodía ya había
hablado con cuatro personas.

El trabajo es bastante sencillo. Atiendo a los clientes, contesto el
teléfono y escribo los correos. No es el trabajo que había imaginado, pero
paga bien y el equipo es simpático.

A las seis terminé y me fui a casa. En el tren pensé que esto puede
funcionar.

stories.title: Dos puntos de vista
stories.text:
Ana y Luis discuten el mismo plan, pero no dicen lo mismo. Ana lo ve claro
y Luis tiene dudas.

—Yo creo que el plan es bueno. No veo ningún problema.

—Sin embargo, no estoy de acuerdo. Dudo que funcione en el norte, donde
no hay tren.

—Aunque no tengas razón, puedo entender por qué piensas así. Por eso
quiero discutirlo contigo.

Ana no cambió de opinión. Tampoco era necesario. Hablaron media hora y
al final propusieron trabajar en dos etapas.

Al final los dos tenían razón a medias, que es como suele pasar cuando
alguien discute de verdad.

stories.title: El último autobús
stories.text:
El último autobús de la noche sale a las once y media, y no espera a
nadie. Marta lo sabe, y por eso baja a la parada un cuarto de hora antes
de la hora que le conviene.

Aquel día, sin embargo, se quedó hablando con un hombre mayor que
esperaba el mismo autobús. Hablaron de sus nietos, del barrio, de lo
caro que estaba todo. De pronto el hombre miró el reloj y se puso de pie.

Nos vamos. El último pasa en tres minutos.

Mientras tanto, Marta comprendió que había perdido el autobús. Salió
corriendo y llegó cuando el coche ya estaba arrancando. El conductor la
miró y no dijo nada. Tampoco dijo nada el hombre.

Al final, Marta llegó a casa a las doce menos cuarto. Pensó que había
tenido suerte, y luego pensó que no: para haberlo tenido, había tenido que
perder el autobús primero.

Nunca se lo contó a nadie. No porque le importara el hombre, sino porque
no sabía explicar lo que había sentido al subir. No era alegría, y no era
tristeza. Era otra cosa, y no tenía nombre.

stories.title: ¿Abrir el río?
stories.text:
Hay una compuerta sobre el río, y desde hace veinte años no se abre. En
el pueblo hay dos opiniones, y las dos llevan razón en parte.

Los que sostienen que hay que abrirla dicen que el agua está subiendo y
que dentro de dos años el valle se inundará. Añaden que abrirla es barata
y que nadie tendrá que pagar por ello.

Los que se oponen dicen que la compuerta está vieja, que abrirla cuesta
mucho y que, una vez abierta, no hay forma de cerrar el río otra vez. En
cambio, proponen dejar que el río siga su curso en lugar de construir
más.

El asunto lleva veinte años sin resolverse. En cada reunión alguien
afirma que la vez anterior se llegó a un acuerdo, y alguien recuerda que
no. El acuerdo, si existió, no está escrito en ningún papel.

Es posible que la mejor respuesta sea ninguna de las dos. Es posible
también que sea la de los segundos, y que veinte años de reuniones hayan
sido justo el tiempo necesario.

stories.title: Cómo hacer sopa de verduras
stories.text:
Esta es una receta que funciona en cualquier cocina y no necesita
ningún ingrediente raro.

Primero, las verduras: un puerro, dos zanahorias, una cebolla y un poco de
apio. Puedes añadir otra zanahoria si quieres que quede más dulce.

Segundo, el caldo. Con un litro de agua basta. Si tienes un hueso con
caldo, mejor; si no, con un dado.

Ponlo todo en una olla grande. Añade sal, pero poca: siempre se puede
añadir más después, y quitarla ya no es posible.

Deja que hierva y luego baja el fuego. Cocina despacio una hora. Si
tienes prisa, media hora, pero la sopa será peor. El fuego rápido no
debe hervir: si hierve, la verdura se deshace.

Cuando esté hecha puedes triturarla. No es obligatorio, y mucha gente
prefiere los trozos.

Este es el orden. Si lo inviertes, el resultado es una sopa clara, porque

Por último, la sal. Prueba siempre antes de servir.

stories.title: El turno de noche
stories.text:
El obrero lleva doce años entrando a las diez de la noche y saliendo a
las seis de la mañana, y ya no recuerda qué día es.

Al principio lo contaba. Los lunes, la sirena del puerto le recordaba que
era lunes, y eso bastaba. Después dejaron de bastarle.

El primer mes contaba los coches que pasaban por la avenida. El segundo
mes contaba las luces. Al final del tercero ya no contaba nada y miraba
la pantalla del portátil sin verla, esperando las seis.

Su mujer dice que habla poco. Él dice que no, que habla mucho, que en
catorce años no ha tenido una conversación que no fuera sobre el
dormitorio o la factura. Ella dice que eso no es hablar. Los dos tienen
razón, que es una manera educada de decir que no.

El jueves pasado, a las cuatro de la mañana, se quedó mirando la puerta
cerrada de la sala de máquinas y pensó que hacía diez años que no
miraba. Diez años sin mirar. Después soltó una risa corta, solo, y
siguió trabajando.

A las seis en punto. Se lavó la cara, firmó, salió. El sol estaba
apenas saliendo y los contenedores parecían nuevos. Caminó hasta la
parada y, sin decidirlo, se paró a mirar el mar un minuto. Largo, para
él.

Cuenta los días hasta su cumpleaños
Nunca ha sabido qué día es
Que la sirena le bastaba para saberlo
Que la sirena era demasiado fuerte
Que ya no llega a las diez
Que las luces no le dejaban dormir

stories.title: Por qué hay cola en la panadería

titleTranslations.en: Why there is a queue at the bakery

stories.text:
Hay una panadería en la esquina que tiene casi siempre cola, y hay otra
a cuatro calles que no tiene nunca. La diferencia cuesta tres céntimos.

La primera hace pan todos los días a las cuatro de la mañana. La segunda
llama a un proveedor y lo recibe a las nueve, ya hecho, en el ritmo
apropiado para un local que cierra a las dos.

Esto parece un negocio peor, y lo es, durante las tres primeras horas
del día. Después cambia. El que llega a las siete encuentra las barras
que hizo un panadero, no una máquina. El que llega a las siete a la otra
panadería encuentra el estante vacío y se va.

El dueño de la primera ha calculado mal durante veinte años y bien
durante los cinco últimos, y lo sabe. Dice que la gente no viene a
comprar pan, viene a no tener que decidir.

Su ayudante más joven le dijo una vez que eso no era una panadería, era
una fábrica. El dueño dijo que sí, y que por eso funcionaba.

Hay una cola los lunes que no existe los martes, y no tiene que ver con
el pan. Los lunes el sitio de al lado cierra, y quien iba allí acaba
aquí.

stories.title: Lo que no se dijo
stories.text:
Mi abuelo hablaba poco y escribía menos, y cuando escribía
eran cartas de cuatro líneas que no decían nada y costaban dos horas
de pensar.

Una vez le pregunté por qué no hablaba más. Me dijo que hablar mucho es
fácil, y que hablar poco bien es un oficio. Le pedí un ejemplo. Se
quedó mirando la mesa un rato largo y luego dijo: tú nunca has
preguntado por qué quiero que vengas el domingo. Yo tampoco.

No supe qué decir, y no dije nada, y a él le valió. Ahí está el oficio:
el silencio no es la ausencia de la palabra, es el uso de la palabra
justo cuando no hace falta.

Murió en agosto. En su cajón había ocho cartas sin enviar, y mi madre no
las quiso leer y yo no supe si leerlas. Siguen ahí.

Ahora cuando hablo poco, alguien dice que estoy enfadado. No es eso.
Es que estoy buscando la frase, y la frase no ha llegado, y no quiero
decir la que ha llegado porque la que ha llegado no sirve.

sections.title: Cero a veinte
sections.note: The five hardest: cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve. Drill these.

sections.title: Cien a novecientos

sections.title: Mil y más
sections.note: mil never takes an s and never changes form: dos mil, quinientos mil. It needs 'un' only on its own: un kilo.

sections.title: Tens and one hundred
sections.note: 21-29 are veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés... then it's just the word 'y' + number: treinta y uno.

sections.title: The 'y' rule
sections.body:
Between 31 and 99 Spanish inserts 'y' before the final digit:

treinta y uno (31)
cuarenta y cinco (45)
noventa y nueve (99)

But for 16-29 it's a single word: dieciséis, veintidós. And note 'ciento' shortens before a noun: ciento veinte (120), cien lápices.

sections.title: How hundreds actually work
sections.body:
Below 100 you need 'y' before the last digit. From 100 to 999 the same rule holds, but with -cientos:

doscientos (200)
doscientos cincuenta (250) — not 'doscientos y cincuenta'
quinientos noventa y nueve (599)
novecientos noventa y nueve (999)

Then it resets to plain arithmetic:

mil (1000)
dos mil (2000)
diez mil (10000)
cien mil (100000)
un millón (1000000) — with an accent

Watch the two irregular spellings: quinientos has a q and no c, and seiscientos keeps the x. Everything else is mechanical.

explanation.en: Teens and 21-29 are single words; 31-99 use 'y' before the last digit.

questions.prompt: La mochila cuesta cincuenta euros. Todo ___ ciento treinta euros.

options.value: Because hundreds take -cientos and then add the rest directly
Because fifty is a different word after a hundred

explanation.en: The 'y' rule applies to tens and units (treinta y uno), not to hundreds + tens (doscientos treinta y uno — the y does appear there).

lessons.title: Fechas y hora
lessons.subtitle: Counting to a thousand, dates, and telling the time

sections.title: Los mil y más
sections.note: mil is invariable. Only 'un mil' or 'mil' on its own, never 'dos mil' with an s.

sections.title: Los días y los meses
sections.note: Days and months are masculine, and use 'de' before the year: el quince de marzo.

sections.title: La hora
sections.note: es la una (one o'clock) · es la una (one) · a las dos. The hour after 'es' drops the 's'.

sections.title: Telling the time
sections.body:
Spanish builds the time around the half hour:

Es la una. (1:00)
Es la una y media. (1:30)
Es la una menos cuarto. (12:45)
Son las tres. (3:00)
Son las tres y cuarto. (3:15)
Son las tres y media. (3:30)
Son las cuatro menos cuarto. (3:45)

Two things trip people up. First, 'es' only for one o'clock; everything else is 'son'. Second, everything after la una behaves like a plural number, so it takes y: las tres y media, not *la tres y media.

For a date, day first, then 'de' month, then 'de' year:

el quince de marzo de dos mil veinticuatro (15 March 2024)

And a quick note on the big numbers you just learned: for a date you do NOT use y between the hundreds and the tens. Mil ochocientos noventa y cinco = 1895. The y stays because it joins the tens and units, not the hundreds.

sections.title: Ordinals in brief
sections.body:
You will meet these, and they are easier than they look:

primero (1º) · segundo · tercero · cuarto · quinto

From the fourth onwards they are regular -o forms: sexto, séptimo (with an accent), octavo, noveno, décimo.

The 20th and up are plain: el vigésimo segundo = 22nd. From the 30th, el ordinal is exactly the tens word plus -ésimo: el trigésimo (30th), el cuadragésimo (40th).

Notice that only three of the six endings are unique:

-AR verbs:  yo -o   tú -as   él -a   nosotros -amos   vosotros -áis   ellos -an

- 'o' covers yo only.
- 'as' and 'áis' cover tú and vosotros.
- 'a' covers él.

Learn -ar and you're 80% of Spanish.

-AR:  o, as, a, amos, áis, an
-ER:  o, es, e, emos, éis, en
-IR:  o, es, e, imos, ís, en

-er and -ir share the first three and the last two. Only nosotros and vosotros differ. So a new -ir verb is nearly free once you know comer.

sections.title: ser vs estar
sections.body:
The single hardest pair in Spanish:

ser → who you are. Soy feliz. (I am happy — permanently.)
estar → where you are. Estoy feliz. (I am happy — today.)

Same sentence, two meanings. If swapping the verb changes the meaning, use estar.

So: Soy de Londres. (I am from London.) Estoy en Londres. (I am in London right now.)

sections.title: How reflexives actually work
sections.body:
A reflexive verb points the action back at the subject. The infinitive ends in -se, but that -se is not a word you say. It splits into a pronoun that goes in front:

levantarse → me levanto · te levantas · se levanta
nos levantamos · os levantáis · se levantan

Three things to notice:

él and ellos share se, because Spanish does not mark gender here. That is not a mistake.

The nos- and os- forms are identical to the plain verb: nos levantamos, os levantáis.

Many reflexives take a preposition rather than a direct object, and that preposition often carries meaning in English that surprises you:

acostarse a las once (to bed at eleven) · ducharse con agua fría
levantarse de madrugada (get up at dawn)

You can spot a reflexive by the pronoun sitting in front of the verb. If you see me, te, se, nos or os before a verb, look for a reflexive.

lessons.title: Verbos con infinitivo

sections.title: The two phrases
sections.note: Both take the infinitive, unchanged — never conjugated.

sections.title: Plans, obligations, and offers
sections.body:
Spanish uses the infinitive for things you have not done yet. There are no 'will' or 'must' endings on the verb:

ir a + infinitive — I'm going to, I'll
Voy a estudiar. (I'm going to study.)
Vamos a ir. (We're going to go.)

tener que + infinitive — I have to, I must
Tengo que trabajar. (I have to work.)
Tienes que venir. (You have to come.)

Two more worth learning:

querer decir — to mean
¿Qué quieres decir? (What do you mean?)

poder + infinitive — to be able to, can
¿Puedes ayudarme? (Can you help me?)

Note the word order: the auxiliary goes in front, the infinitive stays bare. Tener is conjugated, but estudiar never is.

There is also hay que — 'you have to', impersonal, for rules that apply to everyone:

Hay que pagar. (You have to pay.)

lessons.subtitle: What happened, and it is finished

sections.title: hablar y comer
sections.note: Three endings carry almost all of it: -é/ió for yo and él, and -aste/iste for tú. Nosotros still adds an ending: hablamos, comimos.

sections.title: Reading the endings
sections.body:
Once you know three endings you can complete any regular preterite:

-AR:  habl-é · habl-aste · habl-ó · hablamos · hablasteis · hablaron
-ER:  com-í · com-iste · com-ió · comimos · comisteis · comieron
-IR:  viv-í · viv-iste · vivió · vivimos · vivisteis · vivieron

-ar verbs and -er/-ir verbs differ only in the yo and tú endings, and even then they rhyme: é/aste against í/iste.

The preterite is for events with a beginning and an end. 'I spoke' is done: hablé. That is the whole difference from the imperfect, which is lesson 2.

questions.prompt: Which nosotros form is correct for hablar?

lessons.title: El imperfecto
lessons.subtitle: Habits, backgrounds, and no clear end

sections.title: hablar, comer, vivir
sections.note: This one is almost free: -er and -ir share every ending, and nothing changes except in three verbs.

sections.title: What the imperfect is for
sections.body:
The imperfect describes things with no clear start or end: habits, states, backgrounds, and things going on while something else happens.

-AR:  habl-aba · habl-abas · habl-aba · habl-ábamos · habl-abais · habl-aban
-ER:  com-ía · com-ías · com-ía · com-íamos · com-íais · com-ían
-IR:  viv-ía · viv-ías · viv-ía · viv-íamos · viv-íais · viv-ían

Only three verbs are irregular: era (ser), iba (ir), veía (ver).

The test is the English one. 'I used to live there' is imperfect: Yo vivía allí. 'I lived there for three years' is a completed stretch, so preterite: Viví allí tres años.

With two verbs in one sentence, put the background in the imperfect and the event in the preterite:

Llovía cuando salí. (It was raining when I left.)

questions.prompt: Which is the imperfect of ser?

lessons.title: Elegir la forma
lessons.subtitle: Preterite or imperfect? A decision you can actually make

sections.title: The decision
sections.body:
There is no rule you can apply mechanically. But there are patterns:

Use the PRETERITE when the action:
· is a single completed event (fui, hablé, compré)
· has a clear start and end (trabajé seis meses)
· is stated as a fact (Ayer llegué tarde.)
· is a series of events in sequence (llegué, comí, volví)

Use the IMPERFECT when the action:
· describes a habit (hablaba todos los días)
· describes a background state (era pequeño)
· sets the scene for another action (llovía cuando...)
· has no stated end (vivía en Madrid)

Mixed sentences are the interesting case. The imperfect is the scenery, the preterite is the event:

Hacía sol cuando salimos. (The sun was shining when we left.)

And note the asymmetry in the trigger words:

siempre, nunca, a menudo, todos los días → usually imperfect
ayer, anoche, la semana pasada, el año pasado → usually preterite

siempre is the exception that proves the rule. 'Siempre fui feliz' is a fact about a whole stretch of life, so preterite. But 'Siempre cantaba' is a habit, so imperfect.

sections.title: Two verbs for 'was'
sections.body:
Spanish has no single 'was'. Which one you use decides whether the sentence reads as background or as an event:

Era pequeño. — He was small. A lasting fact, so imperfect.
Estaba cansado. — He was tired. A temporary state, so imperfect.
Hubo un problema. — There was a problem. A single event, so preterite.

And a useful pair of formulas for the story tense:

De pequeño, jugaba en la calle.
Al día siguiente, me mudé de ciudad.

The first sets up a background with the imperfect. The second moves the story forward with the preterite. Reading them together is how the past becomes narrative rather than a list.

sections.title: The future attaches to the infinitive
sections.body:
This is the one place in Spanish where the ending goes onto the whole infinitive:

hablar + é = hablaré
comer + é = comeré
vivir + é = viviré

That is why the future of hablar is hablaré and not hablé — hablé is the preterite, which you already know. The two look almost identical and mean completely different things:

Hablé con ella. (I spoke to her. Done, in the past.)
Hablaré con ella. (I will speak to her. Later.)

The endings, for all three patterns:

-é · -ás · -á · -emos · -éis · -án

hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablaréis, hablarán
comeré, comerás, comerá, comeremos, comeréis, comerán
viviré, vivirás, vivirá, viviremos, viviréis, vivirán

Two things to watch. The endings attach to the whole infinitive: hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablaréis, hablarán., unlike the present where él is habla. Second, there is no irregular yo form in the future at all — unlike the present, where half the verbs have one.

sections.title: Two futures for one meaning
sections.body:
Spanish has two ways to talk about the future, and the difference is small.

ir a + infinitive — for plans you have already made
Voy a estudiar. (I'm going to study.)
Vamos a ir a la playa. (We're going to go to the beach.)

el futuro — for predictions, promises, or the plain future
Va a llover. (It is going to rain. / It will rain.)
Estudiaré más. (I will study more.)

In conversation the difference is often nil: 'I will come' can be iré or voy a ir. Use whichever sounds better, and default to ir a for arrangements:

Voy a llamar al médico. (I'm going to call the doctor. — decided)
Llamaré al médico. (I will call the doctor. — promised)

Adverbs of likelihood sit neatly here:

Seguro que llamaré. (I will definitely call.)
  Probablemente llamaré. (I will probably call.)
  Quizá llame. (Maybe I'll call.)

Notice quizá usually takes the subjunctive (it can take the indicative when the speaker is more certain) — 'maybe I'll call' as a guess, not a plan. You'll meet that in lesson 4.

sections.title: The most useful tense you have not met
sections.body:
The conditional does one job very well: it softens a sentence. Spanish uses it where English uses 'would', 'could', 'should' and 'may'.

¿Podrías abrirme la puerta? (Could you open the door?)
Me gustaría un café. (I would like a coffee.)
Deberías descansar. (You should rest.)
Vamos a la playa, ¿verdad? — Sí, preferiría no ir. (I'd rather not go.)

The endings are identical for every pattern:

-ía · -ías · -ía · -íamos · -íais · -ían

hablaría, hablarías, hablaría, hablaríamos, hablaríais, hablarían

Two notes on form. yo and él share: hablaría, hablaría.. And the conditional has no irregular verbs whatsoever — poder is podría, not *poderia, and ir is iría.

Unlike the future, the conditional is not a tense about the future. It is a mood for attitude: what you would do, could do, should do, might do. That is why it turns up in the next lesson inside if-clauses, where it does its real work.

lessons.title: Si + condicional
lessons.subtitle: The if-clause English speakers get wrong

sections.title: Two kinds of if
sections.body:
English splits its if-clauses in two: 'if it rains, I will stay' (real) and 'if I had money, I would travel' (unreal, past). Spanish does not. It uses the same shape for both, and the difference is only which tense goes in the if-clause.

REAL — the if-clause is present, the result is future:

Si llueve, no saldremos. (If it rains, we won't go out.)
Si no vienes, iré solo. (If you don't come, I'll go alone.)

HYPOTHETICAL — the if-clause is imperfect subjunctive, the result is conditional:

Si tuviera dinero, viajaría. (If I had money, I would travel.)
Si fuera más tarde, me iría a casa. (If it were later, I would go home.)

This is the part that feels strange at first: 'if I had money' in English uses had, but Spanish uses tuviera — the imperfect. You already know the imperfect from chapter 3, so you are equipped.

A few shapes worth knowing:

si no — if not: Si no llueve, iremos.
cuando — when (also takes the two tenses): Cuando llegue, te llamo.
Cuando era niño, jugaba fuera.
mientras — while: Mientras esperamos, hablamos.
a menos que — unless: Iré a menos que llueva.

And one asymmetry to watch: Spanish has no 'if + would'. The would part goes in the main clause, never after si.

sections.title: A pattern to steal
sections.body:
The hypothetical form is enormously useful for anything you would like but cannot have:

Me gustaría viajar más. (I would like to travel more.)
Si pudiera, viajaría más. (If I could, I would travel more.)

Viviría en el campo. (I would live in the countryside.)
Si viviera en el campo, no trabajaría tanto. (If I lived in the countryside, I wouldn't work so much.)

Notice that the verb being conditionalised changes between the two sentences. Si + imperfect is not a fixed phrase with one verb; it pairs with whatever verb the sentence is about.

sections.title: Hacer does three unrelated jobs

One of the most useful verbs in Spanish, doing three jobs that have nothing to do with each other.

Weather also borrows it: Hace mucho calor, hace frío.

Hace dos años que no lo veo. (I haven't seen him for two years.)

2. as a light verb: hacer + noun, meaning to do or make something.

Hacer la cena. (To make dinner.)
Hacer ejercicio. (To exercise.)
Hacer un viaje. (To take a trip.)

3. obligation and need: hay que, hacer falta, tener que, deber.

Hay que pagar. (One has to pay.)
Va a hacer falta. (It is going to be needed.)
Hace falta llamar al médico. (The doctor needs to be called.)

And deber:

Tienes que ir. (You have to go.)
Debes ir. (You must go.)
Deberías ir. (You should go. — conditional, softer)
Debo ir. (I must go.)

groups.title: Identity

sections.title: Two rules that settle most sentences
sections.body:
Rule one, identity. If the sentence could be answered with a name, a place, or a job, it wants ser. Soy Ana. Es de Lima. Es médico.

Rule two, time. If you could put today, right now, or at the moment in front of it, it wants estar. Estoy en casa. Estoy cansado. Está cerrado.

Neither verb is the default. Spanish does not use estar because it is closer to English, and it does not use ser as a catch-all. Choosing between them is a judgement about what the sentence is claiming, which is why this is the chapter where people get stuck.

lessons.subtitle: Where things are and how they are going

sections.title: estar
sections.note: Fully irregular, and shaped differently from ser in the past.

sections.title: Adjectives for estar
sections.note: None of these describe what something is. All describe how it is going.

sections.title: What estar adds
sections.body:
estar covers four things, and none of them is identity.

Location. El libro está en la mesa. La librería está en la calle.

Condition. La puerta está rota. El café está frío.

Mood. Estoy contento. Está triste.

Progress. Estoy comiendo. Está trabajando.

That last one has no English equivalent. Spanish marks an action in progress with estar plus a gerund, where English needs an auxiliary: I am eating, you are working. The gerund is the -ando and -iendo forms, added straight onto the infinitive.

comer → comiendo, hablar → hablando, dormir → durmiendo, pedir → pidiendo

Note the spelling rule for the -er and -ir gerunds. Drop the e or the final vowel of the infinitive, then add -iendo. That is why it is yendo and not *iendo, and why dormir gives durmiendo rather than *dormiendo.

Locative estar also has an irregular form worth learning now, because it carries a preposition: está de vacaciones, está de viaje. The same está covers both being at a place and being on holiday.

sections.title: The distinction, in one question
sections.body:
Ask yourself whether the location is a permanent fact about a place, or a temporary position of a thing.

Permanent fact about a place, and estar still wins. España está en Europa.

Temporary position of a thing, so estar is the only option. El libro está en la mesa.

The trap is that big places blur this. Madrid está en el centro sounds right, and so does Madrid es en el centro. Both are accepted. But Mi casa está en Madrid cannot become Mi casa es en Madrid, because a house is not a location, it is a thing sitting at one.

When in doubt with a building or an object, use estar. It is never wrong for an exact position.

sections.title: What does not change
sections.body:
Most adjectives mean the same with either verb, and Spanish does not care which you pick.

Es simpático and está simpático. Both work. Es alto and está alto. Both fine.

Only a handful genuinely flip meaning, and the table above lists them. Learn those as pairs and stop worrying about the rest.

There is also a group where the adjective itself changes shape with estar, and this is a real trap:

La puerta está rota. → La puerta está rota. The adjective is the same.

But compare:

Está aburrido. He is bored now.
Se aburre. He gets bored.

Es aburrido. He is boring.

The first pair differs only by verb. The second differs by verb and by adjective form, and neither is interchangeable with the other.

sections.title: Quality against process
sections.note: An adjective tells you what something is like. A verb tells you what happens.

sections.title: Why this distinction is useful
sections.body:
The adjective describes a state. The verb describes an event.

Es aburrido says people find him dull, full stop. No change, no story.

Se aburre says something happened. He was fine, then he got bored. That is a narrative, and it is why chapter 3's two past tenses become natural here.

Estaba aburrido toda la tarde. He was bored all afternoon. A state, all day.

Se aburrió después de comer. He got bored after lunch. An event, one point in time.

Two verbs worth pairing deliberately:

acordarse and olvidarse are opposites and both take de. Me acuerdo de la cita. Me olvidé de la cita.

aburrirse and despertarse are not opposites but pair naturally, because they describe a change of state in someone. One happens to you, the other brings you back.

sections.title: Two families of state
sections.body:
Spanish sorts physical and mental states across two verbs, and English collapses both into be.

Physical and involuntary, with tener. Tengo hambre. Tengo sed. Tengo sueño. Tengo miedo. Tengo fiebre.

Mood and condition, with estar. Estoy cansado. Estoy contento. Estoy enfermo.

The overlap is where mistakes happen, because several states could belong to either family. The differences are real but small:

tengo hambre — I am hungry. A physical need.

estoy hambriento — I am starving. A state of being, more dramatic.

tengo sueño — I am sleepy. The urge.

estoy cansado — I am tired. The condition after the fact.

You can be tired without being sleepy, and the two words say so. The same split runs through miedo and anxiety.

The other use of tener is with nouns in general, where English also uses have. Tengo un perro. Tengo veinte años. Tengo prisa. Tengo razón.

sections.title: Weather, and how you ask
sections.body:
Spanish divides weather between hacer for temperature and the weather verbs for precipitation.

Hace calor. Hace frío. Hace buen tiempo. Hace mal tiempo.

Llueve. Nieva. Está nublado. Hace sol.

The verbs llueve and nieva look odd in the table because Spanish only uses the third person. You say llueve, never lluevo. This is the same in English when you say it rains, never it rains.

To ask the weather, take the third person singular and move the stress one syllable to the end:

Llueve. → ¿Llueve? (five syllables to six, stress to the end)

Nieva. → ¿Nieva?

Making it windy or sunny:

Hace viento. It is windy.

sections.title: Why Spanish has four words for meals
sections.body:
English collapses the day into three meals. Spanish names them by when they happen, and the names are useful because they tell you the hour.

Desayuno. Breakfast, and by extension the morning. Also la mañana, which is the same part of the day.

Almuerzo. Lunch, and by extension the early afternoon.

Merienda. The mid-afternoon snack. This is the one that catches people: merienda can be a coffee and a pastry, or it can be the meal you have instead of a formal dinner. It is not a formal word, and outside Spain and Latin America most learners never meet it.

Cena. Dinner, but note the trap. In Spain cena is at nine or ten in the evening. In Latin America la comida is the main evening meal, at eight or so, and cena is lighter. The words moved; the times stayed.

Two phrases worth knowing whole:

tener hambre — to be hungry

tener sueño — to be sleepy

Neither takes an article, and neither uses estar. Desayuno porque tengo hambre. Ceno porque tengo sueño.

sections.title: Two articles worth memorising
sections.body:
You already know the pattern: nouns ending in -o are masculine, nouns ending in -a are feminine, and the article matches.

el queso, la carne, el pollo, la verdura.

Two nouns break it, and both are worth learning now rather than meeting them in a shop.

La leche. Feminine, without exception: la leche, las leches, una leche fría.

El agua. Feminine noun, masculine article only because it begins with a stressed a. El agua. But because it is feminine it takes an adjective in the feminine: el agua fría, not *el agua frío. And if you add another noun it becomes las aguas, which then agrees: las aguas limpias.

The rule behind both: a singular noun ending in a pronounced -e takes el in the singular, whatever its gender. Plural la is unaffected.

For ordering food, you will not go far with grammar. You point, or you say lo mismo, y otra vez.

sections.title: How firm you sound
sections.body:
Four ways to order the same soup. All of them are correct; they differ in how much you are asking rather than demanding. Spanish does not read any of them as rude.

Neutral — just name the dish. No verb at all.

La sopa, por favor.

This is the normal way to order in Spain. It does not sound blunt, and adding a verb is not more polite.

With querer — the everyday middle.

Quiero la sopa, por favor.

Correct and common. Slightly more assertive than naming the dish, because now you are the one who wants.

With the conditional — the safe choice.

Me gustaría la sopa.

Chapter 4's conditional, and the one to reach for with someone you do not know. Me gustaría la sopa, por favor is unremarkable; it is not effusive.

With poder, also conditional — the most careful.

¿Podría traerme la sopa?

Note the pronoun after the verb: podría traerme, not *podría me traer. This is what you use when you are asking a favour rather than placing an order.

sections.title: The whole conversation
sections.body:
A full exchange, so you can see where each phrase sits.

— Buenas noches. ¿Qué va a tomar? (Good evening. What are you having?)
— Para mí, una sopa y el pescado. ¿Y usted?
— El pollo con arroz, por favor. Y un agua.
— Muy bien. Un momento.

Note the first question. Qué va a tomar is not what are you drinking, it is what are you having, and it covers the whole meal. The verb is ir, in the third person, because Spanish makes no distinction between you and usted here. Compare usted va and tú vas.

Then the bill. La cuenta, por favor. Not la factura, which is the invoice, and never el cuenta.

And the tip. La propina is optional in Spain and expected in much of Latin America, usually around ten per cent. If you leave it, you say gracias por la propina, or simply gracias.

One phrase to recognise but not use yourself. Buen provecho is said to someone else about their meal. If someone says it to you, that means they think you are eating well.

Where is the bakery?

Está al lado de. It is next to.

Está enfrente de. It is opposite.

sections.title: Asking and paying
sections.body:
Two questions cover nearly every shop.

How much is it? ¿Cuánto cuesta? Note the singular cuesta for one thing. Plural cuestan.

Do you have this? ¿Tiene esto? Note the usted form tiene, which is what you use with a shopkeeper.

For an exact amount, Spanish uses the same structure as everything else: verb, number, noun.

Dos kilos de naranjas. (Two kilos of oranges.)

Cuatro cajas de leche. (Four boxes of milk.)

The plural noun with a number stays singular. Un kilo de naranjas, not *un kilo de naranja.

Paying. You say the amount you are handing over and ask for change:

— Sesenta euros, por favor. ¿Tiene cambio?
— Sí, aquí tiene.

Paying by card: Pago con tarjeta. Paying in cash: Pago en efectivo.

And a very common one you will hear: es un regalo. It is a gift. If someone says that as they hand you something, do not pay.

sections.title: Talking about weather
sections.body:
Asking is the same question from chapter 5, with the stress moved to the end.

¿Qué tiempo hace? — What is the weather like?

Answering takes two halves, and they use different verbs.

Hace frío y está nublado. It is cold and cloudy.

Hace calor y hace sol. It is hot and sunny.

Llueve, pero no hace frío. It is raining, but it is not cold.

Note that weather is very often about you. Está bien para salir means it is fine for going out, which is a question about plans rather than meteorology.

The temperature pattern is worth knowing. Hace calor in the afternoon, hace frío por la noche. Inland Spain has exactly this shape: hot afternoons and cold nights. The coast is milder, and hace bueno means pleasant rather than merely good.

Two useful phrases for complaining and predicting:

Hace un frío horrible. It is horribly cold.

Va a hacer frío. It is going to be cold. Va a plus an infinitive, from chapter 4.

sections.title: How to tell a story about your day
sections.body:
You have all the pieces now. Here is the pattern, and it is the one you will use most often.

Me despierto a las siete. (I get up at seven.)

Me ducho enseguida. (I shower right away.)

Desayuno café con leche. (I have coffee with milk for breakfast.)

Trabajo hasta las seis. (I work until six.)

Vuelvo a casa. (I get home.)

Ceno y me acuesto a las once. (I have dinner and go to bed at eleven.)

Four things make this sound Spanish rather than a word-for-word English translation.

First, reflexivity. Me despierto, not *despierto. The pronoun is doing the work here, not the ending.

Second, omission. You can drop the pronoun when it is obvious. Trabajo hasta las seis needs no me, because the person is the subject.

Third, time goes before the verb when the time is the new information. A las seis vuelvo. Vuelvo a las seis. Both work, but the second buries the time.

Fourth, contrast. Antes (+) did one thing, ahora (+) does another. Antes vivía en el campo; ahora vivo en la ciudad.

And for anything you have not done yet, chapter 4's future. Mañana voy a trabajar.

sections.title: Why the prepositions split
sections.body:
English leans on one preposition for all of this: work AS a nurse, study FOR medicine, study medicine. Spanish uses three, and the split is not along the lines you would expect.

trabajar de + profession. Trabajo de panadero. No article, ever.

estudiar para + a career. Estudio para ser abogado. This is the preposition for the goal, not the subject.

estudiar + subject, with no preposition. Estudio derecho, or just estudio. If you say what you study with no article, Spanish reads it as the bare thing itself.

ser de + place, for origin. Soy de Sevilla. Chapter 5 already warned about this: estar is where you are now.

One useful contrast while you are here. trabajar en is where you work, and it takes no profession: trabajo en una panadería. So the same sentence can carry the two together: trabajo de panadero en una panadería.

What time do you start?

Two phrases worth having whole:

estar de alta — to be signed on, employed

estar de baja — to be signed off, on sick leave

Both use de, and both are about status rather than place. Estoy de alta desde marzo.

And the word for the floor, which is not in this chapter: el piso is used in Spain for both storey and flat, which trips up anyone reading a Spanish letting agency.

sections.title: The hardest little idea in the chapter
sections.body:
Spanish has three sets of pronouns and this is the one nobody expects. It marks the indirect object: the person who receives something, or the subject of a verb like gustar.

me, te, le, nos, os, les.

Note that it is le, not lo. You already know lo, la, los, las for the direct object. The dative is a different set with different forms, and mixing them up is the single most common error at this stage.

Placement, in two rules.

Before the conjugated verb: Le doy el libro. Le doy a él el libro.

Attached to the infinitive or the gerund, at the end: Voy a darle el libro. Estoy dándole el libro.

One accent to watch. When the pronoun is attached to an infinitive, the infinitive loses its accent: hablar becomes hablarle, not hablárle. The two together form one word, and Spanish marks the stress on the whole thing.

The other half of the idea, which chapter 6 already used without naming it: gustar works backwards. Me gusta el café. Literally, coffee is pleasing to me. So the person who feels something is the dative, not the subject: Me gusta, te gusta, le gusta, nos gusta, os gusta, les gusta.

That one shift explains a lot of chapter 5 as well. Me gusta la idea is not about gustar at all; it is estar with a dative in front.

sections.title: The order English gets wrong
sections.body:
Four of these verbs want the thing first and the person second, and Spanish does not move them.

Explico el problema a Marta. I explain the problem to Marta.

In English you can put the person first and it still reads fine. In Spanish the verb is followed by its direct object, and the indirect object comes after that. Putting the person in the middle is not a stylistic choice; it is a different sentence.

The exception is when the person is already a pronoun. Then you can go round the front.

Explico el problema a Marta. Le explico el problema.

And when you do that, the pronoun comes before the verb rather than attached to it, because there is no infinitive to attach to.

Two more worth knowing:

preguntar por is asking about something in general. Pregunto por el salary.

preguntar para is asking on someone's behalf. Pregunto para Marta.

That distinction has no English equivalent and it is the difference between asking about something and asking for someone.

sections.title: The accent you only need for this
sections.body:
Three verbs of asking and telling take a little enclitic that pulls the stress onto the second syllable.

preguntar — pregúntale, pregúntame

decir — dile, dígame

buscar — búscame

The accent is not decoration. Preguntale would stress the last syllable and sound wrong. With one pronoun it is compulsory; with two it becomes optional, and you will see both.

One rule worth learning properly, because it explains the whole pattern: Spanish has a stress rule that almost always puts the stress on the last syllable that can take it. An infinitive ending in -ar counts as stressed already (hablar is ha-BLAR), so nothing else can take the stress. An infinitive ending in -er or -ir is weak, so a following word can pull it: hablar MÉ, ver a-SÍ, escribir a-QUÍ.

So the same thing happens everywhere. DÍ-le-melo. MÁ-nda-me-lo. Á-bre-me-la-luz.

And that is why the plural stresses on the final syllable and needs no accent: díganme, pregúntenle, búsquenme. When the stress lands on the last syllable of a word ending in a vowel or n, no accent is written.

sections.title: Which a is which
sections.body:
Spanish has three ways to attach a time to a clause, and picking the wrong one is common enough to be worth sorting out once.

A + article, for a point. A las nueve. Llego a las nueve.

De ... a, for a span. Trabajo de nueve a cinco. Llego a las nueve y me voy a las cinco.

Desde and hasta, for a start or an end on their own. Trabajo desde las nueve. Trabajo hasta las cinco. Desde 2019.

The article is the tell. If both ends have las, you are naming two moments. If neither does, you are describing a continuous stretch. Llego a las nueve y salgo a las cinco is two events. Trabajo de nueve a cinco is one long one.

Now the trap, and it is a genuine one. Todo el día and todos los días look almost identical and mean opposite things.

Trabajo todo el día — I work all day.

Trabajo todos los días — I work every day.

One is duration, the other is frequency, and the only difference is whether the article is singular or plural. Chapter 6's shopping lesson already used this pair for the same reason.

Frequency, while you are here, and all of it takes todos:

todos los días, todas las semanas, todos los meses, todos los años.

sections.title: Marks, and the word everybody gets wrong
sections.body:
The vocabulary is easy; two words in it are not.

aprobado and suspendido are adjectives. You are aprobado, you are suspendido. But you are also given a nota, a mark, out of ten.

He aprobado la examen — wrong twice. Examen is masculine: el examen.

He aprobado el examen — right.

Suspenso is the verdict: you say saqué un suspenso, not *soy suspenso. Es aprobado/suspenso — and note there is no article. You do not say *está aprobado.

Two more distinctions worth having.

aula is the classroom in secondary school and university. clase is the lesson, the group, or the classroom in primary school. Una clase de historia is a class of history. The two words overlap more in Spain than in Latin America.

And el carné is the word for the card that proves something, not the card itself: el carné de conducir is a driving licence, el carné de estudiante is a student card. The word you want for an identity document is el documento de identidad, or simply el DNI, which everybody uses regardless of what the paper says.

When it comes to marks, and this trips up English speakers constantly: a mark of six is not a failure in Spain. A dos is a clear fail. A cinco is the pass mark. A diez is perfect.

sections.title: One word, four jobs
sections.body:
Chapter 2 introduced the reflexive se. The impersonal is a different se, or rather the same letters doing something else, and it is how Spanish says things English needs a whole auxiliary for.

The idea: the subject is nobody in particular, or everybody, or the situation itself. Spanish does not invent a dummy subject, so it reaches for se.

se habla, se vive, se habla inglés

It is spoken. It is lived. English is spoken.

In English these get do, people, or nothing at all. Spanish has one word for all of it, and the verb is third person singular whether you like it or not. Se habla, never *hablan.

The other three jobs, so you can tell them apart.

Passive: se construyen los puentes. The bridges are built.

Reflexive, which chapter 2 covered: se lava todos los días. He washes every day.

Accidental: se me cayó el libro. The book fell on me. This is the one English cannot do at all, and it is everywhere. Se me olvidó, se nos cayó, se te cayó el café.

The distinguishing test is what is missing from the sentence. If there is a real subject somewhere, it is passive. If there is no subject at all, it is impersonal. If there is a pronoun doing something to someone, it is accidental.

The pronoun that surfaces in the accidental is a dative, which is why chapter 7 needed the dative first. Se me cayó is literally it fell to me.

sections.note: Same verbs you already know, in a mood you do not. The -ar and -er endings differ; -er and -ir are identical.

sections.title: What changes and what does not
sections.note: The endings change. The stem usually does not, which is why the tables look familiar.

groups.title: An -ar verb
groups.note: -ar takes e, es, e, emos, éis, en in the subjunctive. The stem is untouched.

groups.title: An -er verb
groups.note: -er and -ir both take a, as, a, amos, áis, an.

groups.title: With ojalá
groups.note: ojalá takes the subjunctive and nothing else. There is no indicative form of ojalá.

groups.title: Without ojalá
groups.note: querer QUE also takes the subjunctive. Chapter 4's future is untouched by any of this.

sections.title: Why there is a second mood at all
sections.body:
Every tense so far has one job: report what you know is true. Hablo, tengo, hablo mañana. All of those are things you can be sure of, or at least are stating flatly.

The subjunctive is for everything else. Wishes, doubts, feelings, things you want, things you are not sure of, things that are somebody else's opinion. In Spanish this is a whole second set of endings.

The endings are worth learning as one shape rather than three, because -er and -ir are identical and only -ar differs.

-ar: hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen

-er and -ir: tenga, tengas, tenga, tengamos, tengáis, tengan

If you can say "tenga" you can say "pueda", "sepa" and "venga". One set of six covers almost everything you will meet.

ojalá is the easiest way in, because it takes the subjunctive and nothing else, and it has an accent that stays there in every form: ojalá, ojalá viniera, ojalá no llueva.

Ojalá se followed by the imperfect is the tense you will see most: ojalá fuera, ojalá tuviera, ojalá pudiera. That is not the same ojalá as chapter 4's, because the verb behind it is in a past mood. For now, present subjunctive after ojalá is the useful one: ojalá entienda.

Two more to have ready. esperar QUE, from chapter 4's reading, takes the subjunctive: espero que vengas. And no creo que, which takes it too: no creo que sea verdad. Both are lesson 2.

sections.title: creer, pensar, dudar
sections.note: creer and dudar are the ones that flip. pensar only changes shape, not mood.

sections.title: Same verb, two moods, different meaning
sections.note: This is the heart of it. Whether the clause after que takes the subjunctive is what tells you who is being reported and how sure anyone is.

groups.title: My own belief
groups.note: When you report your own belief, you are stating a fact about what you think. Indicative.

groups.title: Someone else's belief
groups.note: Negation is what flips it. No creo que venga means I do not think he is coming.

groups.title: Doubt either way
groups.note: dudar QUE always takes the subjunctive. Whether you doubt or not is the whole signal.

groups.title: Expectation
groups.note: esperar QUE, from chapter 4's reading. Hope and expectation behave like doubt.

groups.title: Fear
groups.note: tener miedo DE que. The de is not optional: tengo miedo de que venga.

sections.title: The rule that is nearly a rule
sections.body:
There is a single pattern behind almost every use, and once you see it the rest is detail.

If the main clause is about YOUR certainty, your feeling, your wish or your opinion, the clause after que takes the subjunctive.

Creo que viene — I think he is coming. Your belief. Indicative, because you are reporting what you know.

No creo que venga — I do not think he is coming. Your belief, negated. Subjunctive, because now you are reporting what someone else said or what you doubt.

Dudo que venga. Subjunctive.

Espero que venga. Subjunctive.

Tengo miedo de que venga. Subjunctive.

Me alegro de que venga. Subjunctive.

Es una pena que venga. Subjunctive.

In English all six of those are flat declaratives with no mood change at all. Spanish has to mark the shift, and it marks it with the verb.

So the practical test is short. Ask yourself: am I stating something, or am I reporting somebody's view, including my own doubt? Statement means indicative. Report means subjunctive.

Three traps.

The negative can sit anywhere. No creo que venga, but also Creo que no viene — that one is indicative and means I think he is not coming. The negation matters where it sits, not merely that it exists.

que is not always followed by the subjunctive. Creo que es verdad is fine, and correct: you are stating what you believe as a fact about the world. It is only when the belief itself is the subject that the mood shifts.

And cuando means when, not because. cuando + indicative, porque + indicative. Do not carry the subjunctive across from one to the other.

lessons.title: Que: causa, propósito, concesión
lessons.subtitle: One word, three jobs

sections.title: The same word doing three things
sections.body:
que introduces a clause. What that clause does depends entirely on the word in front of it, and this is where Spanish feels hardest to an English ear because English has three separate words.

As cause: No trabajé porque llovía. I did not work because it was raining.

As purpose: Salgo para que puedas descansar. I am going out so that you can rest.

As concession: Aunque no importaba, lo hice. Although it did not matter, I did it.

That is three jobs for one word, and the verb mood partly disambiguates. Purpose and concession lean on the subjunctive; plain cause stays indicative.

Salgo para que puedas descansar. Subjunctive, because the rest is not yet a fact.

Salgo porque llueve. Indicative, because the rain is.

Though you can have porque + subjunctive too, and then you are reporting somebody's explanation rather than asserting your own: Dice que no viene porque está cansado. He says he is not coming because he is tired. Here the porque clause carries his reason, so it takes the subjunctive for the same reason esperar que does.

This lesson has no verb table, and that is the point. The grammar you need here is not conjugation but word choice, and the fastest way to learn it is to read the four words around the que and ask what they mean.

groups.note: Reporting a reason, so the whole clause shifts. Same word, different mood.

groups.title: So that
groups.note: para que is always subjunctive. The purpose is by definition not yet real.

groups.note: para + infinitive is purpose without a subject. Use this when you do it yourself.

sections.title: Four ways to give a reason, by how formal they are

groups.title: Spoken
groups.note: The default. Works in any register, and the only one of the four that works inside a question.

groups.title: Neutral
groups.note: Slightly more formal. Common in speech, and it can start a sentence.

groups.title: Formal
groups.note: Written and business. Also the only one that works as a concession too.

groups.title: Formal, and causal
groups.note: Given that. Emphasises that the cause is already established, so nobody argues with it.

groups.title: Not a cause
groups.note: por qué carries the accent and asks a question. porque never does.

sections.title: Puesto que does two jobs
sections.body:
The four cause connectors are interchangeable in meaning, and they differ in register and in one genuine ambiguity.

porque — neutral, the one you will use most. Works at the start of a sentence, in the middle, and in a question.

ya que — a shade more formal. Especially natural at the start: Ya que estamos aquí, podemos hablar.

puesto que — formal, common in writing and in business. And this is the interesting one: puesto que can also mean since/taking into account, so it concedes as well as causes. Puesto que no hay nadie, vámonos — since there is nobody, let us go. That reading takes the indicative, because it is stating a fact rather than reporting a belief.

dado que — formal and strictly causal. It presents the cause as settled, which is why it suits written argument.

Two things people get wrong.

The accent. por qué with an accent is a question. porque without one is a conjunction. There is no correct form of porque with an accent.

And the position. Only porque is fully free. The other three tend to go at the front of a sentence, where a comma is optional: Puesto que es tarde, nos vamos.

A practical note on register. Learners who write only porque are never wrong. Learners who use puesto que in conversation sound like a contract.

lessons.title: Aunque
lessons.subtitle: Concession, and the subjunctive that comes with it

groups.title: Conjunction
groups.leftTranslation: Although I do not like it, I am going.
groups.note: The default. Takes the indicative for a fact, and the subjunctive for a supposition.

groups.title: With a noun
groups.left: A pesar de la lluvia, salí.
groups.note: a pesar de + noun, no clause. The noun keeps its article.

groups.title: With a clause
groups.left: A pesar de que llovía, salí.
groups.note: a pesar de que + clause. The verb is in the indicative when the cause is a fact you assert.

groups.title: Literary
groups.left: Si bien es cierto, no lo es del todo.
groups.note: si bien, and it usually sits at the start of a sentence.

groups.title: However
groups.note: Not a conjunction: it cannot join two clauses, it stands alone. Chapter 4's reading uses it.

sections.title: The mood does the work
sections.body:
The single most useful thing about Spanish aunque is that the mood tells you how real the thing being conceded is.

Although it is raining — I know it is raining. Hecho, so indicative.

Aunque llueva, saldré — even if it rains, I will go out. The rain is hypothetical, so subjunctive.

Although I may be wrong — nobody is claiming to be wrong; it is being entertained. Subjunctive.

That last pair is the whole lesson. Two sentences that look identical in English differ by one letter, and the difference is whether you are asserting or supposing.

English handles this with a modal hedge — "although it may be" — where Spanish just changes the verb.

A second trap. Sin embargo and no obstante are not connectors. They cannot join two clauses: *Aunque no me gusta sin embargo voy is not a sentence. They need their own clause and a full stop or a comma.

And a third. a pesar de takes a noun, a pesar de que takes a clause, and the difference is exactly the que:

A pesar de la lluvia — in spite of the rain.

A pesar de que llovía — although it was raining.

Leave the que out and you have a different sentence, or no sentence.

sections.title: Two of these need a conjunction and two do not

groups.title: So that
groups.note: así que and por eso both work alone. You cannot join two clauses with them.

groups.title: Therefore
groups.note: Por lo tanto and en consecuencia are the formal pair, and also stand alone.

groups.title: And so
groups.left: Estaba lloviendo y así que no fui.
groups.note: Watch the y: así que arrives after the conjunction, never fused to it.

groups.title: The exception
groups.note: por lo que is different: it joins two clauses, and it means the reason, not the consequence.

sections.title: Consequence, cause, and the pair that catches people
sections.body:
Four phrases mean so, and they are interchangeable in meaning. What differs is register and whether they can join two clauses.

así que — spoken and written. The most common of the four.

por eso — spoken and written, and more emphatic than así que. Por eso no fui: I did not go *for that reason*, which implies the reason matters.

por lo tanto and en consecuencia — formal. Same thing, both stand alone.

None of them joins two clauses. If you want the two clauses in one sentence, you need y: Entonces no fui. Así que no fui. Y así que no fui.

The pair that catches everyone is por eso and por lo que.

por eso — consequence. No fui, por eso. I did not go, and that is the consequence.

por lo que — cause, and it DOES join clauses. No fui por lo que llovía. I did not go because it was raining.

Same preposition, same words, opposite meaning, and one of them takes a clause while the other takes a comma. When you see por lo, check for the que.

Two connectors that are not so at all, which is the useful thing to remember about them:

además — besides that, and it adds rather than concludes.

por otra parte — on the other hand, and it introduces the opposing side of an argument. Together they are how you build both sides of a point, which is exactly what chapter 9's reading does.

sections.title: Three ways to say the same passive

groups.title: With ser
groups.note: The formal and literary one. News, history, obituaries.

groups.title: With se

sections.title: The participle, and the one form that changes
sections.body:
A participle is a third kind of word form, after the infinitive and the two moods you know. Spanish has two of them, chosen by the infinitive's ending: -ado for -ar, -ido for -er and -ir. Construido, not construído, even though the infinitive is construir.

Most participles are regular. Enough that you can guess one you have not seen.

The irregular ones are worth learning as words, which is why they are in the lesson above: dicho, hecho, puesto, visto, escrito, abierto, roto, resuelto.

Three passives, and the choice is register rather than meaning.

ser + participle is formal. News and history: El puente fue construido en 1985.

se + participle is ordinary and far more common in speech. El puente se construyó en 1985. Same sentence, same meaning.

tener + participio is a state rather than an event. Tengo el informe hecho means the report is done, not that somebody did it.

The trap with se + participle: the verb agrees with the subject, not with a passive. Los puentes se construyen. Puente is singular in the sentence and construyen is plural, because the subject is plural. This is the exact opposite of ser, where El puente fue construido keeps the participle agreeing with the subject too — so both agree, but for different reasons.

And do not confuse se + participle with the impersonal se from chapter 7. Se habla inglés has no participle and no object. Se construyen los puentes has both, and the verb agrees with the subject. Chapter 7's four uses of se become five.

lessons.title: La posición de lo destacado
lessons.subtitle: lo, la, le — putting the emphasis first

sections.title: Moving the pronoun to the front

groups.title: Direct object
groups.note: A direct object pronoun moved to the front for emphasis. It stays a pronoun: lo, not el libro lo.

groups.title: Indirect object
groups.note: With a fronted dative you usually need the se, and the direct object moves with it.

groups.title: Reflexive
groups.note: Reflexives rarely move. The emphasis goes on an added phrase instead.

groups.title: The pronoun never becomes a noun
groups.note: You cannot put the noun back after fronting: *El libro lo compro el libro is not a sentence.

sections.title: What is actually going on
sections.body:
Spanish can move a pronoun to the front of the sentence when the thing it refers to is the new information.

Compro el libro. — I buy the book.

El libro lo compro. — It is the book I buy, not something else.

English does this with a cleft sentence or with intonation. Spanish does it by word order, and the moved pronoun stays a pronoun: lo, never el libro.

Which pronoun moves. Direct objects (lo, la, los, las) move freely. Indirect objects (chapter 7's le, les) also move, but a reflexive clitic usually cannot — Me ducho por la mañana, not *Por la mañana me ducho, which sounds wrong to a Spanish ear. Emphasise a reflexive with an added phrase instead.

The awkward case is a moved dative alongside a moved direct object, and Spanish solves it with se: El libro se lo doy. That se is not reflexive and not impersonal; it is a placeholder so the two pronouns do not collide. You will meet it again in chapter 9.

One thing this is not. It is not word order generally. Spanish is not a topic-prominent language the way Japanese is, and moving a pronoun to the front does not grant you freedom over the rest of the sentence. Compre el libro lo compro yo is not a sentence. Move the pronoun, and leave the rest where it was.

sections.title: Said and unsaid
sections.note: In longer text the important information is usually the part nobody says. Both columns are true; only one of them is what the writer is doing.

groups.title: Plain statement
groups.note: Stated outright. Rare in fiction, and its absence is usually deliberate.

groups.title: Action instead
groups.right: Marta comprendió que había perdido el autobús.
groups.note: The fact is still there, but it arrives as a conclusion she draws. The reader does the work, which is why the reader remembers it.

groups.title: Mood, with no adjective
groups.right: No era alegría, y no era tristeza.
groups.note: Twice we are told what the feeling is not, and the feeling is never named. That is the whole ending.

sections.title: Three things to look for
sections.body:
Comprehension questions ask for facts, and facts are the easy half. The other half is what the writer arranged for you to work out.

First, negation of the obvious. No era alegría, y no era tristeza is not a fact about Marta; it is the writer declining to name something. If a text tells you twice what a thing is not, the thing is the point.

Second, the noun that does not belong. In the bus story the driver and the grandchildren each pass through in a single sentence. Neither is what the story is about. Look for the noun that recurs, or that the last paragraph comes back to.

Third, how firmly the speaker holds their position. Afirmar, sostener and matizar are three different levels of commitment, and a text that uses all three is making a point about how people argue. That is the whole of the river story: the first side afirma, the second matiza, and the narrator ends by suggesting that neither answer is right.

One practical habit. When a question says why, the answer is usually not in any single sentence. Read the paragraph before and the paragraph after, and ask what the writer needed the reader to assume.

lessons.title: El registro
lessons.subtitle: Formal and informal, and how to tell

groups.title: Neutral
groups.right: La reunión empieza a las nueve.
groups.note: Works anywhere. The default, and the safest place to start.

groups.title: Formal
groups.right: La sesión comienza a las nueve.
groups.note: Usted, wider vocabulary, longer sentences. News, contracts, anything signed.

groups.title: Colloquial
groups.right: ¿La reunión empieza a las nueve, no?
groups.note: Tú, contractions, and a rising tone on the tag at the end. Two friends, a shop, a bar.

sections.title: Four tells, and they travel together
sections.body:
You do not need a dictionary of slang to tell registers apart, because register leaves four marks and they almost always appear together.

First, usted or tú. Es la señora is formal; eres tú is not. A shop says ¿qué desea? rather than ¿qué quieres? for exactly this reason.

Second, the mood. La reunión es a las nueve is neutral and formal, because it asserts a fact in writing. La reunión empieza a las nueve is what you would say out loud, in any register.

Third, vocabulary width. Empezar is neutral; comenzar is formal; arrancar is spoken. Descansar is formal for a siesta and echar una siesta is not.

Fourth, sentence shape. Formal Spanish writes long subordinated sentences. Spoken Spanish splits them and uses short ones. The bus story is short sentences; the river story is long ones with commas.

One warning. These are tendencies, not rules. A shopkeeper will say llámame in a formal context, and a lawyer will say te lo mando in an informal one. What matters is consistency inside a text, not which register you chose.

And one place where the two meet: sin embargo is fine in speech, and puesto que is not. Some forms travel between registers and some do not, and the ones that do are the ones you pick up first.

lessons.title: Palabras por sufijos
lessons.subtitle: -mente, -ción, -dad, -oso, -ero

sections.title: Words built on them
sections.note: Every one of these you can now build something else from.

groups.title: -mente
groups.note: Adverb from an adjective, and formed on the feminine whatever the adjective is: lenta + mente. Adverbs do not change after this.

groups.title: -ción
groups.note: A noun for an action or a quality, and always feminine. So is -dad.

groups.title: -dad
groups.note: Directly from the adjective, with nothing in between, and also always feminine.

groups.title: -oso
groups.note: An adjective meaning full of something, or tending towards it. Dangerous, dark, lazy. Darkness of mood is not peligroso.

groups.title: -ero
groups.note: One who does the thing named before it, and also the shop where it happens: el panadero is the baker and the bakery.

sections.title: How far this gets you
sections.body:
This is the most useful thing in the chapter for reading without stopping to look things up, because a suffix tells you what kind of word you are holding before you know what it means.

-ción and -dad are feminine nouns. Know the suffix and you know the article, without understanding the word at all.

-oso is an adjective, so it agrees with the noun beside it: un problema oscuro, una solución oscura. If a word ends that way and the noun changes gender, the suffix is the clue that it has to.

-mente is an adverb, and adverbs do not change. Lento becomes lentamente once and then stays that way.

Two warnings.

The first is that the gender rule has exceptions you learn as words, not as rules: el agua and el mapa are masculine, la mano and la foto are feminine, and no suffix predicts either.

The second is that -oso does not mean one thing. It means full of something, or tending towards it. Un río peligroso is a river full of danger, not a dark river.

An exercise for this chapter. Take a page you have not read before and underline every word ending in -ción, -dad, -mente or -oso. You will have marked most of the nouns, adverbs and adjectives on the page without understanding one of them.

lessons.title: Los prefijos
lessons.subtitle: des-, in-, con-, sub-, super-

sections.title: What each one tends to do
sections.note: Tends to. Prefixes are the least reliable part of the system, and the exceptions are worth more than the rule.

groups.title: des-
groups.note: Also undoing an action, and sometimes a plain negative. Desayunar is not a negative of anything, though.

groups.title: in-
groups.note: The most reliable of the five: inútil, incorrecto. The exception worth knowing is infancia, which is not a negative of anything.

groups.title: con-
groups.note: Contar is to count, not to count together. Con- also makes the intensive forms: comer became conmigo.

groups.title: sub-
groups.note: Usually spatial and usually exact. Submarino means under the sea and nothing else.

groups.title: super-
groups.note: Often better rather than merely higher: superior means both at once.

sections.title: Prefixes are the weakest rule in the language
sections.body:
Suffixes are close to reliable. Prefixes are not, and the reason is worth knowing before you rely on them.

The problem is that pre- and sub- and con- arrived in Spanish at different times, from Latin and then from French, and each layer kept its own habits. A prefix that looked obvious to a speaker two centuries ago often looks arbitrary now, and nobody feels the need to change it.

So learn two of the five well and distrust the rest. In- before an adjective is the one you can rely on: inútil, incorrecto, imposible. Sub- before a noun is the second: el submarino, el subterráneo.

Des- is the interesting one, because it does three different jobs. It undoes something (desmontar, take apart), it reverses an action (descansar, the opposite of cansar), and it is sometimes just a negative (descubrir, which is not a negative of anything at all).

One more worth knowing, because it is not on any list: many Spanish verbs carry a prefix that has no English equivalent and no systematic meaning. Madrugar is to get up early, and there is nothing in the madrug- that means early.

A useful caution for the reading chapter that follows. When you meet an unfamiliar word, check the suffix first, because the suffix is reliable. Only then look at the prefix, because the prefix may be telling you nothing.
